VISIT-01.cite: Alhassan Sowe field visit, Manduar (Brikama), 8 Nov 2026: 1 farmer interviewed, 7 fields seen, 5 recorded.

IMERG-POWER.cite: GPM IMERG daily precipitation retrieved through the NASA POWER API at the pilot point, 2015-2025; dry day = below 1.0 mm; July-September window.

MERRA2-POWER.cite: NASA POWER MERRA-2 PRECTOTCORR at the pilot point, 2015-2025 (0.5 x 0.625 degree).

MODIS-NDVI.cite: MODIS MOD13Q1 250 m NDVI, good-quality composites only (reliability 0), 2015-2026, via the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service.

GIEWS25.cite: FAO GIEWS Country Brief, The Gambia, 22 May 2025: maize planting starts late May; rice, millet and sorghum planting begins June with the seasonal rains.

GIEWS25B.cite: FAO GIEWS Country Brief, The Gambia, Feb 2025 (archive): maize harvested from September; rice, millet and sorghum harvested October to November.

GIEWS26.cite: FAO GIEWS Country Brief, The Gambia, 28 Jan 2026: 2025 cereal harvest completed Dec 2025; heavy Aug-Sep rain caused flooding and delayed harvests; local maize prices are monitored.

GIEWS02.cite: FAO/GIEWS Africa Report No. 3, Dec 2002, p.33: groundnut, the main cash crop, fell by more than half in 2002 after a 3-5 week dry spell from late June to early August reduced the area planted.

GIEWS97.cite: FAO/GIEWS Foodcrops and Shortages, The Gambia, 20 Nov 1997: rain stopped in mid-July, stressing early maize and millet; virtually all maize was lost despite rain returning in mid-August; aphid damage to millet and groundnut; Striga upsurge; downy mildew on maize and millet.

MWG16.cite: Gambia National Multidisciplinary Working Group, Early Warning Bulletin 2016/16 (1-10 Oct 2016): 'Philippine pink' groundnut harvested across the country in early October; other varieties vary by variety and sowing date.

MWG18.cite: Gambia National Multidisciplinary Working Group, Early Warning Bulletin 2018/15 (21-30 Sep 2018): weaver birds (Quelea quelea) attack mainly rice and early millet; farmers bird-scare from early morning to late evening; blister beetle damages early millet, notably in West Coast Region.

BAG00.cite: Bagayoko, Buerkert, Lung, Bationo, Roemheld (2000) Plant and Soil 218:103-116, doi 10.1023/A:1014957605852 (Niger and Burkina Faso): legume/cereal rotations increased cereal yields at all sites; topsoil mineral N was higher after legumes, more so after groundnut than cowpea; nematodes were lower in rotation sorghum than continuous sorghum.

BAG01.cite: Bagayoko, Alvey, Bationo (2001) Causes of legume-rotation effects in increasing cereal yields across the Sudanian, Sahelian and Guinean zone of West Africa: after groundnut, rotation cereals gained 26-85% total dry matter vs continuous cereals in year 4; cowpea effects on millet were much smaller.

BUE02.cite: Buerkert, Piepho, Bationo (2002) multi-site time-trend analysis of soil fertility management, West Africa (510-1300 mm rain, sandy soils): legume-rotation effects tended to increase over time but were strongly species-dependent.

JAS00.cite: Journal of Agricultural Science, Cambridge 134:277-284 (2000), doi 10.1017/S0021859699007650 (sandy soil, semi-arid West Africa): continuous pearl millet yielded less than legume-millet rotations; legume yields were consistently lower in monoculture than when rotated with millet; organic matter declined under continuous millet and under cowpea-millet and groundnut-millet rotations.

ADE-GJAS.cite: Adetumbi et al., Ghana Journal of Agricultural Science 55(2), doi 10.4314/gjas.v55i2.5 (60 seed growers, 26 Gambian communities): groundnut is the principal export crop (about 66% of agricultural export earnings); the seed system is predominantly informal; Fleur-11 is among the most promising varieties.

GGP.cite: West Africa Groundnut Germplasm Project, third annual report (regional): 100-120 kg of pods are needed to sow one hectare; farmers struggle to keep seed through the season; foliar diseases and rosette are common constraints; about 30% of production is eaten at home and 60% traded.

MEDWIN.cite: Improved Maize Varieties: Enhancing Food Security in Rural Communities of Central River Region North (Gambia), doi 10.23880/fsnt-16000339: Gambian agriculture is rain-fed; improved maize varieties supplied to smallholders mature in about 85 days (Kabamano 80-100 days).

CSA18.cite: FAO, ICRISAT, CIAT (2018) Climate-Smart Agriculture in the Gambia, CSA Country Profiles for Africa: rain-fed low-input systems; fertiliser use about 6 kg/ha, about half the West Africa average; soils poor in organic matter with runoff and erosion; land share millet 24%, groundnut 23%, rice 15%, maize 8%, sorghum 7%, pulses and vegetables under 1%; rice, sorghum, millet and maize mostly for home use; groundnut the major cash crop; millet in the Sahelian zone only intermittently because of bird damage; legume rotation, composting and groundnut IPM listed as climate-smart practices.

BADU.cite: Badu-Apraku et al. (IITA preprint 202002.0409): maize in West and Central Africa is constrained by drought, low soil N and Striga; extra-early (85-90 days) and early (90-95 days) hybrids exist; maize responds strongly to N.

MENKIR.cite: Menkir A. (Cambridge University Press, online 5 Feb 2009) Response of early maturing maize landraces and improved varieties to moisture deficit: early maturity helps escape drought, but yield losses can be large if drought occurs from just before flowering to the start of grain filling.

GHANA25.cite: Springer s44372-025-00370-6 (Ghana, 2025): nitrogen is the most limiting macronutrient for maize; yield rose with N rates up to 120 kg N/ha; N use efficiency is often low.

SINGH.cite: Singh B.B., Indian Journal of Genetics and Plant Breeding 76(4): cowpea is inherently tolerant of drought and heat and fixes nitrogen in poor soils; 60-75 day varieties are released in 45+ countries; thrips and Maruca are major pests in sub-Saharan Africa; Striga in Sahel and savanna, Alectra in Guinea and Sudan savannas.

ELEWA08.cite: Elewa, J. Applied Biosciences 10(2), 2008: cowpea can fix about 60-70 kg N/ha for the following crop (literature value, site dependent); phosphorus is limiting in many tropical soils.

FTF23.cite: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Legume Systems Research, final report Dec 2023: smallholder cowpea yields in West Africa are typically 10-20% of potential because of insect pests, pathogens, parasites and drought; early released varieties mature in about 65-70 days.

ABDOU-NIGER.cite: Abdou S., INRAN Niger, J. Applied Biosciences: early cowpea lines average 61.6 days to 50% maturity; early maturity lets cowpea escape terminal drought and late-season insects; fodder is also produced.

TROPFOR.cite: Tropical Forages fact sheet, Cenchrus americanus (pearl millet): perhaps the most drought-tolerant grain species; best on sandy or light loam soils; maturity mostly 75-180 days; straw has uses as bedding, thatching, fencing and fuel.

IRD.cite: IRD study, Sine-Saloum (Senegal): early millet 'Souna' cycle about 95 days when sown in the first 10 days of June, about 85 days when sown in late July; sandy 'dior' soils are easy to work but have mediocre moisture retention and fertility.

PMREV14.cite: Pearl millet production practices in semi-arid West Africa: a review, Experimental Agriculture (2014): millet is grown on predominantly sandy soils; Striga build-up is linked to low fertility, drought and continuous planting of millet and other host cereals.

CRM22.cite: Climate Risk Management 36 (2022) 100436 (Senegal): early planting (1-10 June) improved sorghum, millet and groundnut yields at 9 locations; millet performed better than sorghum or groundnut under a mid-century climate scenario.

FARMPEDIA.cite: Edross S. (2025) Sesame as a drought-resistant crop, Farmpedia (University of Guelph): early types mature in 95-110 days; flowering from 35-45 days after planting; shattering and seed loss if left standing.

SESAME-REV.cite: Review of sesame production (encyclopedia.pub entry 66936): nearly all varieties shatter; manual harvest raises costs; pre-harvest losses up to 50% reported; drought at vegetative and flowering stages limits yield.

AUBEE02.cite: Aubee E. and Hussein K. (2002) Emergency relief, crop diversification and institution building: the case of sesame in The Gambia, Disasters 26(3), doi 10.1111/1467-7717.00213 (abstract read): a Catholic Relief Services sesame programme in The Gambia ran for more than 25 years.

AFLA-PREP.cite: Ghana groundnut aflatoxin review (preprint 202407.2235): hazards include rain at harvest and drying, drying on bare ground, storing on bare floor and long delays before stripping; traditional harvest, drying and shelling are labour-intensive; haulm is in high demand as livestock feed.

POINT22.cite: The Point (Gambia), 5 Sep 2022: aflatoxin has lowered the value of Gambian groundnut exports; an official said groundnut is banned in Europe and goes to China as feed; an official also said fertiliser is costly and some farmers cannot afford it.

HAULM26.cite: Adewuyi, Camara, Dauda (2026) Groundnut haulm as livestock feed and its marketing in Kanifing Municipality and Brikama, The Gambia (106 respondents at Abuko and Brikama Kraal markets): haulm is traded as feed (78.6% of traders mix it with wheat bran) with constraints of price, transport, storage and season.

UMN.cite: IAPRI/UMN working paper 78 (Zambia): relative to maize, groundnuts are more labour intensive, especially for weeding, harvesting and shelling.

JFP.cite: Journal of Food Protection (White Rose eprint 111288): earlier Gambian research found high aflatoxin in groundnut-based sauces; contamination is typically higher in dry-season storage; fertilisation, insect control, drying and sorting reduce it.

water_requirement.note: Needs a local source (NARI or extension).

drought_tolerance.note: A 3-5 week dry spell in late June to early August 2002 cut national groundnut output by more than half, mainly by reducing the area planted.

nitrogen_fixing.note: Topsoil mineral N was higher after groundnut than after cowpea in West African trials.

nutrient_demand.note: Legume; local fertiliser and phosphorus needs still to be sourced.

ground_cover_erosion.note: Needs a source. Lifting the crop at harvest disturbs the soil; to confirm.

household_food_use.note: Manduar farmers grow groundnut for family need and market; it is the major cash crop nationally.

market_access.note: Sold in the local market and to traders. Export value is hurt by aflatoxin (POINT22).

input_cost.note: 100-120 kg of pods are needed per hectare for seed; Manduar farmers use own saved seed or buy at market.

labour_demand.note: Weeding, harvesting, drying and shelling are labour-intensive.

residue_livestock_value.note: Haulm is sold as feed in Brikama markets; animals graze fields after harvest in Manduar.

seed_availability.note: Own saved seed or market. The seed system is informal (ADE-GJAS), so quality is a risk.

planting_months.note: Manduar farmer: late July. Planting is rain-dependent; late June to early August dry spells can delay it (GIEWS02).

harvest_months.note: Early November in Manduar; 'Philippine pink' types are harvested in early October nationally.

pests_diseases.value: leaf spot and rosette (regional), aphids, aflatoxin in storage

good_after.note: Legumes yielded less in monoculture than when rotated with a cereal (millet) on sandy soil.

avoid_after.note: Repeated groundnut: legume yields were consistently lower in monoculture.

_meta.note: Reported as grown by Manduar farmers (VISIT-01).

n_credit.note: Reference: rotation effect on mineral N was larger after groundnut than cowpea.

water_requirement.note: Local evidence of drought vulnerability exists (GIEWS97) but a water requirement figure is still needed.

drought_tolerance.note: In 1997 rain stopped in mid-July and virtually all maize was lost even though rain returned in mid-August. The stage from just before flowering to early grain filling is the most sensitive.

nutrient_demand.note: Nitrogen is the most limiting nutrient; Manduar farmers buy urea.

household_food_use.note: Maize is mostly produced for home use in The Gambia.

market_access.note: Mostly grown for home use; local maize prices exist. Manduar farmers did not name maize as a main market crop.

input_cost.note: Farmers reported urea at about GMD 2,000 (unit to confirm); fertiliser is costly and use is low.

residue_livestock_value.note: Animals graze fields after harvest in Manduar; stover value to confirm.

seed_availability.note: Own saved seed or market. Improved early varieties are supplied through projects (MEDWIN).

planting_months.note: Manduar: July. Nationally planting starts from late May.

harvest_months.note: Manduar: October. Nationally harvest starts in September.

pests_diseases.value: Striga, downy mildew, drought at flowering

good_after.note: Cereals grew better after groundnut in West African trials (millet and sorghum were tested; maize is assumed similar).

avoid_after.note: Continuous cereals yielded less and can build up Striga.

_meta.note: Reported as grown by Manduar farmers (VISIT-01).

drought_tolerance.note: Still lost part of the crop in the 1997 mid-July stop (GIEWS97).

nutrient_demand.note: Best on sandy or light soils (TROPFOR); fertiliser need not sourced.

labour_demand.note: Farmers bird-scare from early morning to late evening; harvest and threshing add labour.

seed_availability.note: Farmers said they would consider millet; seed access not yet confirmed.

avoid_after.note: Continuous cereals: lower yield and Striga build-up.
